The LORD Gave, and the LORD Hath Taken Away
thuh LORD GAYV and thuh LORD hath TAY-kun uh-WAY
n. phr. (Job's confession at the loss of all he had)
Hebrew YHWH nāthan wa'YHWH lāqāch — nāthan, to give, and lāqach, to take, set side by side under one Subject; the AV keeps the bare parallel and adds nothing to soften it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The words are Job's, spoken standing, with his mantle rent and his head shaven, in the hour the messengers finished their report: oxen and asses driven off, sheep burned, camels taken, and all ten children dead under a fallen house. He does not say that the Sabeans took, or the Chaldeans, or the wind from the wilderness, though each had done its work. He names one Giver and one Taker and they are the same Person. This is not resignation to fate and it is not stoicism; the next clause is blessed be the name of the LORD, which is worship, and the verse after it records that in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly. The confession rests on two things Scripture holds together without embarrassment. The first is that everything Job had was given, never owned absolutely — children, flocks and health alike came out of the open hand of God and were held on His terms. The second is that the hand which gives is the hand which takes, and that it remains righteous in both motions. Job later speaks rashly and is answered out of the whirlwind, but he is never reproved for this. It stands as the church's pattern for bereavement: not the denial of grief, for Job rent his mantle, but grief that bends the knee.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Give, to bestow; to confer without compensation. Take, to receive what is offered, or to seize, to lay hold on. Job 1:21, the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away.

expand to see more

Give, to bestow; to confer without price or compensation.

Take, to lay hold on; to receive back what was lent or lodged.

Hebrew nāthan, to give, bestow, deliver up.

Hebrew lāqach, to take, fetch, lay hold of.

Bless, to praise; to glorify for benefits received. Job 1:21.

Key Scripture

Job 1:21 — "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Job 1:22 — "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly."

Job 2:10 — "But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips."

Jam 5:11 — "Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy."

Modern Corruption

The saying is quoted as a shrug at impersonal fate, and the doctrine behind it — that God Himself ordains the taking — is traded for a God who merely permits and is as surprised as the mourner.

expand to see more

The common modern use empties the line of its Subject. It is offered at funerals as a way of saying that life gives and life takes, that these things happen, that the universe turns. Job says the opposite. He names the LORD twice and makes Him the agent of both verbs, and it is precisely because a Person and not a process stands behind the loss that the sentence can end in blessing. One cannot bless a process. The comfort in the verse is not that loss is natural but that it is governed, and governed by One whose name Job already knows.

The second corruption is more respectable and more damaging. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) and the wider evangelical instinct that God only permits what He does not will would have us say that God did not take Job's children, that Satan did, and that God was grieved alongside Job as a fellow sufferer. The narrative forbids it. Satan acts only within a boundary God sets and twice extends, and the inspired verdict on Job's confession is that he sinned not, nor charged God foolishly — which would be a strange verdict if he had just attributed to God a work God did not do. A God who merely permits cannot be blessed for the taking, and the mourner who is told so is left with grief and no one to worship in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nāthan, to give, and lāqach, to take — one Subject governs both verbs, and the clause that follows is blessing, not complaint.

expand to see more

Hebrew nāthan, to give, bestow, set, deliver.

Hebrew lāqach, to take, seize, fetch, receive.

The verbs share one Subject: the covenant name, YHWH.

Naked came I out of my mother's womb is the premise — nothing was owned, all was lent.

Blessed be the name of the LORD is the conclusion; the verse ends in worship, Job 1:21.

Usage

"the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD"

"in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly"

"shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?"
